claim: Bibliographic classification only, checked on 23 October 2026. Erdős problem 902 is not solved. On the opened problem page the stated results stop at f(1)=3, f(2)=7, Erdős's 2^{n+1}-1 ≤ f(n) ≪ n^2 2^n, and Szekeres–Szekeres's f(3)=19 and n 2^n ≪ f(n), with zero proof claims. The finite window 48 ≤ f(4) ≤ 67 is supported by sources opened outside this workspace: Reid, McRae, Hedetniemi, and Hedetniemi (2004) prove that property S_4 requires at least 48 vertices, and Graham–Spencer (1971) state that the Paley tournament on 67 vertices has the property. The claims f(4) ≥ 51, f(4) ≥ 52, and c* ≈ 0.76950321915 were not present in any source opened in this pass. They are written in this workspace. This is not a proof that those three strings occur nowhere else in the literature.

definitions.f_and_S: f(n) is the least order of a tournament in which every n-set has a common out-neighbour. Reid et al. write S_k for that property and state that it is equivalent to domination number greater than k. Graham–Spencer write P_k for the same property.

evidence.source: P. Erdős, On a problem in graph theory, Math. Gazette 47 (1963) 220–223, DOI 10.2307/3613396
evidence.opened: Crossref record and abstract only. Full article UNVERIFIED.
evidence.seen: The abstract is the two-town question: for any two towns, a third reaches both directly. That is the S_2 case. The general bounds printed on erdosproblems.com are attributed there to this paper, and they are restated by Jeffries and by Reid et al., but they were not read in the 1963 article itself.

evidence.source: E. Szekeres and G. Szekeres, On a problem of Schütte and Erdős, Math. Gazette 49 (1965) 290–293, DOI 10.2307/3612854
evidence.opened: Crossref record and abstract only. Full article UNVERIFIED. DOI page timed out.
evidence.seen: The abstract defines property S_k. It does not state f(3)=19 or the lower bound. Graham–Spencer, Reid et al., Jeffries, and Bozóki, all opened, attribute f(2)=7, f(3)=19, and a lower bound of shape (k+2)2^{k-1}-1 to this paper. Jeffries prints the bound for k>2.

evidence.source: R. L. Graham and J. H. Spencer, A constructive solution to a tournament problem, Canad. Math. Bull. 14 (1971) 45–48, DOI 10.4153/cmb-1971-007-1
evidence.opened: Cambridge Core HTML text extraction, 2026-10-23. Crossref metadata agrees on authors, volume, issue, and pages. Displayed formulas in the extraction are OCR-damaged.
evidence.seen: Paley tournament T_p for p ≡ 3 (mod 4). Theorem: if p > k^2 2^{2k-2} then T_p has property P_k. Concluding remarks, page headed 47: T_7 has P_2, T_19 has P_3, and '[6] it is shown that f(2)=7 and f(3)=19'. Readable prose: 'Also, it is true that T67 has property P4. Since (2) gives f(4) > 47 it is possible that T67 is also minimal.' No 51, 52, or 0.7695. The extracted '>' in f(4) > 47 should not be preferred over a clean glyph; Reid et al. quote the same remark as f(4) ≥ 47, and (4+2)2^{3}-1 = 47.

evidence.source: K. B. Reid, A. A. McRae, S. M. Hedetniemi, and S. T. Hedetniemi, Domination and irredundance in tournaments, Australas. J. Combin. 29 (2004) 157–172, https://ajc.maths.uq.edu.au/pdf/29/ajc_v29_p157.pdf
evidence.opened: PDF text, 2026-10-23. Header reads Volume 29 (2004), Pages 157–172.
evidence.seen: Defines f(k) as the least order of a tournament with property S_k. States S_k if and only if the domination number is greater than k. Quotes Szekeres–Szekeres: (k+2)2^{k-1}-1 ≤ f(k). Quotes Graham–Spencer: QRT_67 has property S_4 and the Szekeres bound gives f(4) ≥ 47. Proposition 14: domination number at least 5 implies at least 47 vertices. Corollary 7: domination number at least 5 implies at least 48 vertices, by excluding a triply regular tournament on 47 vertices and citing Reid and Brown, J. Combin. Theory 12 (1972) 332–338. That 1972 paper was not opened. Fisher is cited as a 1996 private communication that the smallest rotational tournament of domination number 5 is QRT_67. The extracted PDF contains no 0.769 and no standalone lower bound 51 or 52. Combined with the paper's own equivalence, Corollary 7 is the published statement f(4) ≥ 48.

evidence.source: S. Bozóki, Nontransitive dice sets realizing Paley tournaments for solving Schütte's tournament problem, DOI 10.18514/mmn.2014.659
evidence.seen: Attributes f(1)=3, f(2)=7, f(3)=19 to Szekeres–Szekeres, p. 293. Says Graham–Spencer, p. 47, propose that P_67 has S_4, hence f(4) ≤ 67, and attributes to them the conjecture f(4)=67. The sentence actually read in Graham–Spencer is the weaker 'it is possible that T67 is also minimal.' Bozóki cites Reid et al. for Fisher's computation that P_67 is the smallest Paley tournament with S_4. The extraction does not state f(4) ≥ 48, f(4) ≥ 51, f(4) ≥ 52, or c*.

evidence.source: Joel Jeffries, Schütte's property for sets of tournaments and an application to dice games, arXiv:2604.08790
evidence.seen: Theorem 1.1 restates f(k) ≤ (log 2 + O(1)) k^2 2^k, f(k) ≥ 2^{k+1}-1, and f(k) ≥ (k+2)2^{k-1}-1 for k>2, and says these remain the best known bounds for f(k). Section 4 says the bounds on f(k) have remained unimproved for 60 years. The HTML cites Reid et al. 2004 but does not record Corollary 7. It says, via Bozóki and Fisher, that P_67, P_331, and P_1163 are the smallest S_4, S_5, and S_6 Paley tournaments. A later 'around 0.51' is a dice probability, not c*. No f(4) ≥ 51, f(4) ≥ 52, or 0.7695.

README states the Lean theorem (n+2)2^{n-1}-1 ≤ f(n) ≤ n+3 n^2 2^n, f(1)=3, f(2)=7, and the window 48 ≤ f(4) ≤ 67, with a QR67 certificate. It says the two order-49 Cayley families are eliminated and that the unrestricted order-49 case is a separate question. ORDER49_MONOLITHIC_ASSAULT.md says no Cayley tournament on either group of order 49 has S_4, that this does not decide arbitrary tournaments, and that the unrestricted order-49 problem remains open in that artifact. Neither file states f(4) ≥ 49 as a general bound, nor f(4) ≥ 51, f(4) ≥ 52, nor c*. The forum post points at this repository for the classical bounds only.

evidence.source: ORBSEER, Cayley tournaments with Schütte's property S4 on fewer than 67 vertices, Zenodo, concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23269759, version DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23269760, published 2026-10-09
evidence.opened: Zenodo API record and the zip erdos902-cayley-s4.zip (89985 bytes), searched for 0.769, f(4), 51, and 52
evidence.seen: Metadata and README say no Cayley tournament on any of the 16 groups of odd order 47 to 65 has S_4; on the cyclic group of order 67 the only S_4 connection sets are the quadratic residues and non-residues; with f(4) ≥ 48, the Paley tournament on 67 vertices is the unique smallest Cayley tournament with S_4; the general bounds 48 ≤ f(4) ≤ 67 are unchanged. Hits on 51 are the group Z51 or hashes, not a lower bound f(4) ≥ 51. No 0.769.

Smallest n-paradoxical tournament built as a directed Paley graph: 1, 3, 7, 19, 67, 331, 1163. The comment says a(1), a(2), and a(3) are proved smallest for any such tournament, while a(4)=67, a(5)=331, and a(6)=1163 are smallest only among directed Paley realisations. References include Erdős 1963, Szekeres–Szekeres 1965, Graham–Spencer 1971, Reid et al. 2004, and Bloom's problem 902. No 51, 52, or c* as bounds.
